إذا شرح اللاويين كيف يعيش الشعب في حضرة: If Leviticus explains how the people live in God's presence, Numbers explains how this people journeys with God in the wilderness. It organizes the people, reveals the testing of faith, and presents grumbling, rebellion, and judgment, while God's faithfulness to His promise continues. The overall progression is: organization, God's leadership, the testing of faith, then arrival at the boundary of promise.

References: Matthew 4:1-11; 22:37-40; Acts 3:22-23.
الاسم العبري בְּמִדְבַּר (Bemidbar) يعني: The Hebrew name בְּמִדְבַּר (Bemidbar) means “In the wilderness,” and it is taken from the beginning of the book in the wilderness of Sinai. Numbers, or Ἀριθμοί, refers to the censuses, but the census serves the picture of an organized community around the tent of meeting. The two names combine the setting of the events and the organization of the people. Reference: Numbers 1:1-3.
الاسم العبري בְּרֵאשִׁית (Bereshit) يعني: The Hebrew name בְּרֵאשִׁית (Bereshit) means «In the beginning», the word with which the book begins. Genesis means origin, beginning, or formation. The name explains the movement of the book from the creation of the world and humanity to the origin of Jacob's family, which becomes the people of Israel. Reference: Genesis 1:1.
الاسم العبري דְּבָרִים (Devarim) يعني «ك: The Hebrew name דְּבָרִים (Devarim) means “words” or “sayings,” and it is taken from the opening of Moses' address to all Israel. Deuteronomion, however, is associated with the restatement of the law before the new generation, not the presentation of a different law. The people stand on the plains of Moab between the memory of the wilderness and the threshold of the promised land. Reference: Deuteronomy 1:1-5.
الاسم العبري וַיִּקְרָא (Vayyiqrā) يعني: The Hebrew name וַיִּקְרָא (Vayyiqrā) means “And He called,” and it is the opening of the book: “And the Lord called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting.” Leviticus, however, is associated with the Levites and matters of worship and priesthood, although the book directs its teaching to the whole community of Israel. The central question is: How can a sinful people live in the presence of the holy God? Reference: Leviticus 1:1.
الاسم العبري שְׁמוֹת (Shemot) يعني «أسما: The Hebrew name שְׁמוֹת (Shemot) means «Names», the word with which the book begins in listing the Israelites who came to Egypt. Exodus means «departure» or «going out», and summarizes the people's movement from slavery to redemption, from Egypt to Sinai, and from an enslaved community to a people in covenant with God. Reference: Exodus 1:1-7.
الخليقة، السقوط، قايين وهابيل، الطوفان و: Creation, the Fall, Cain and Abel, the flood and the covenant with Noah, the Tower of Babel, the call of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. Genesis is the book of beginnings and promise: God created humanity, humanity fell, but God did not abandon his purpose; rather, through covenant, offspring, and blessing, he began to form a people who would bear his blessing to the world. Reference: Genesis 6–12; 50:20.

Joshua bears the name of salvation and leads into the rest of the land, whereas the New Testament proclaims a deeper rest in Christ; therefore, he is a preparatory historical type, not Christ Himself. References: Joshua 1:9; Hebrews 4:8-11.
المخاطَب هو الجيل الجديد من بني إسرائيل: The audience is the new generation of the children of Israel before crossing the Jordan. Moses brings together history, law, warning, and hope for the renewal of the covenant and the preparation of the people for life in the land, where matters of worship, property, leadership, and justice will arise. References: Deuteronomy 5:1-3; 29:1.

انتهى الخروج بحلول مجد الرب في المسكن، و: Exodus ended with the glory of the Lord coming to rest in the tabernacle, and Leviticus begins from within this presence. Exodus explains how God saved His people and dwelt in their midst, whereas Leviticus answers how the people may approach this holy God. Freedom after redemption is therefore not independence from all authority, but covenant life before God.

بعد الخروج يصل الشعب إلى سيناء، فينتقل ا: After the exodus, the people arrive at Sinai, and the narrative moves from redemption to covenant. God declares that Israel is a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, then gives the commandments. The theological order is important: God saved the people first, then called them to obedience and holiness; the commandment is a response to the covenant relationship, not the price of salvation. References: Exodus 19:3-6; 20:1-17.
بعد قصص القضاة ينتقل السرد إلى ميخا وسبط: After the stories of the judges, the narrative moves to Micah and the tribe of Dan, then to the crime at Gibeah and civil war. The danger begins with the Canaanites and ends in the collapse within Israel itself. The repeated statement summarizes the situation: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.” References: Judges 17:6; 19:1; 21:25.
بعد موت شاول يُمسح داود في حبرون ثم ملكً: After Saul’s death, David is anointed at Hebron and then as king over all Israel; he makes Jerusalem his capital and brings the ark of the covenant there in the proper manner after the incident of Uzzah. In 2 Samuel 7, God declares a covenant with David, linking house, offspring, and throne with a royal hope that expands in the Psalms and the New Testament. References: 2 Samuel 1–6; 7:1-17.
تبدأ الأنساب من آدم وتمتد إلى إسرائيل وي: The genealogies begin from Adam and extend to Israel, Judah, and David, affirming that the exile did not erase the people's identity and did not cut off God's work in history. After the death of Saul, the narrative moves to the union of Israel around David, then to Jerusalem and the ark of the covenant and the organization of priests, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers. References: 1 Chronicles 1–10; 11–16; 23–29.
تبدأ القصة بصلاة حنة في شيلوه وتكريس صمو: The story begins with Hannah’s prayer at Shiloh and Samuel’s dedication to the LORD, then contrasts the corruption of Hophni and Phinehas with the boy’s growth before the LORD. The capture of the ark reveals that the sacred object cannot become a talisman guaranteeing victory; the LORD displays His glory even in the defeat of His people, as shown by the fall of Dagon’s statue before the ark. References: 1 Samuel 1–4; 5–7.

ترفض راعوث العودة وتقول: «شعبك شعبي وإله: Ruth refuses to return and says: “Your people shall be my people, and your God my God,” thus choosing Naomi, her people, and the God of Israel. The two widows arrive in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest, and the story of bitterness gradually becomes a story of fullness. References: Ruth 1:16-17; 1:20-22.
تسقط أريحا بأمر الرب، ثم يكشف فشل عاي أث: Jericho falls at the LORD's command, then the failure at Ai reveals the effect of Achan's sin upon the community, and victory comes after disobedience is dealt with. The Gibeonites, however, enter into a covenant with Israel without seeking the LORD's counsel, and the story affirms that previous experience does not eliminate the need to seek counsel for the present decision. References: Joshua 6–9.
تسقط السامرة أمام آشور نحو 722 ق.م. بعد: Samaria falls before Assyria around 722 B.C. after the accumulation of disobedience. As for Hezekiah, he seeks the LORD before the threat of Sennacherib, and Josiah begins a reform when the Law is discovered and he restores Passover. But the corruption of Manasseh and the continuation of disobedience lead to the fall of Jerusalem, the burning of the temple, and Babylonian exile. References: 2 Kings 17; 18–20; 22–25.
تشكّل الفصح والوساطة والمن والسكنى خلفية: Passover, mediation, manna, and dwelling form an important background for understanding Christ's work in the New Testament, without turning every detail into an independent symbol. The New Testament reads Christ in the light of Passover, connects the water from the rock with Christ, and declares the dwelling of the Word among humanity. References: John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 5:7; 10:1-4.
تظهر خطية العجل الذهبي قبل اكتمال المسكن: The sin of the golden calf appears before the tabernacle is completed, revealing the people's weakness and the covenant's need for God's mercy and Moses' intercession. With the renewal of the covenant, the tabernacle is built, and at the end of the book the glory of the Lord fills the tabernacle. Thus the book moves from the cry of slavery to God's dwelling in the midst of His people. References: Exodus 32–34; 40:34-38.
تظهر مأساة أمنون وثامار، ثم تمرد أبشالوم: The tragedy of Amnon and Tamar appears, followed by Absalom’s rebellion, David’s flight from Jerusalem, and Absalom’s death; the reader sees how the effects of the king’s sin extend into the family and politics. Yet God’s covenant remains in force; David is a repentant king, not a perfect king. References: 2 Samuel 13–20; 22–23.

تقدم الأسفار داود ملكًا ممسوحًا وراعيًا: The books present David as an anointed king, shepherd, and covenant bearer, but they reveal his limitations and create expectation for the perfect king. In the New Testament, Christ comes as the “Son of David” and fulfills what David could not accomplish: He is without sin, and His kingdom does not end in death. References: 2 Samuel 7:12-16; Matthew 1:1; Luke 1:32-33; Acts 2:29-36.
تمتد القداسة إلى الدم والعلاقات والعدل و: Holiness extends to blood, relationships, justice, and love of neighbor, and is summarized by the statement: “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44); likewise, the command occurs: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). The feasts build a memory of God's acts, while the Sabbath for the land and the Jubilee declare that the land belongs to the Lord and that ownership and economics cannot be separated from the covenant. References: Leviticus 17–25.
تنتقل الخدمة من إيليا إلى أليشع، وتظهر م: The ministry passes from Elijah to Elisha, and miracles appear that touch the poor, the sick, and soldiers. In the healing of Naaman, Elisha asks him to wash in the Jordan, and the commander learns that obedience to the word of God is more important than his expectations about how the miracle would occur. References: 2 Kings 2–5.
توضح قصة ناداب وأبيهو أن النعمة لا تلغي: The story of Nadab and Abihu makes clear that grace does not abolish God's holiness and that worship is not a sphere in which people may do whatever they please. Conversely, the renewal of the relationship with the congregation is highlighted through the system of atonement and covenant; thus the book's laws are not to be read as rules separated from God's mercy and presence.
تُفتح أبواب السقوط بكثرة النساء والثروة: The gates of downfall open through the abundance of women, wealth, and alliances, as women turned Solomon's heart toward other gods. After his death, Rehoboam rejects wise counsel, and the people divide into the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah, and Jeroboam establishes the calves for political reasons that become a religious catastrophe. References: 1 Kings 11–12.

راعوث (רוּת؛ Rūt) اسم امرأة موآبية، ولا: Ruth (רוּת; Rūt) is the name of a Moabite woman, and the Old Testament does not provide a certain linguistic meaning for it. What matters is that the literary structure connects the story of a foreign woman to the line of David. Reference: Ruth 4:17-22.

كان أخبار الأيام الأول والثاني عملًا واح: First and Second Chronicles were originally a single work and were then divided into two books. The Hebrew name דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים means “matters of the days,” whereas the Greek name Paraleipomena became associated with omitted matters. Yet the work is not merely a historical supplement; it is a theological rereading of Israel’s post-exilic history, centered on identity, worship, and Davidic hope.
كان الملوك الأول والثاني سفرًا واحدًا في: First and Second Kings were one book in the Hebrew tradition and were later divided. The name מְלָכִים (Melakhim) means “kings,” but the purpose of the book is not merely to recount names; rather, it evaluates kings in the light of the covenant: did the king do what was right in the eyes of the LORD or what was evil? References: 1 Kings 1–2; 2 Kings 25.
كان صموئيل الأول والثاني عملًا تاريخيًا: First and Second Samuel were one historical work in the Hebrew tradition and were later divided into two books. The name is connected with Samuel, and is usually understood in relation to the story of Hannah, who prayed, and God heard and gave her a son; but this does not mean that Samuel wrote both books in their entirety, for the book records his death in 1 Samuel 25. References: 1 Samuel 1:1-28; 25:1.
لا تساوي النجاسة الطقسية دائمًا الخطية ا: Ritual impurity is not always equivalent to moral sin; many purity laws regulate approach to the sanctuary and distinguish between the holy and the common. In Leviticus 16, the high priest enters the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement, bringing together the idea of making atonement for sin and removing it from the congregation. References: Leviticus 10:1-3; 11–16.
لا يخفي السفر سقوط أورشليم وحرق الهيكل و: The book does not hide the fall of Jerusalem and the burning of the temple and the exile, but it interprets this in light of the covenant and the Sabbath rest of the land, and then ends the work with the decree of Cyrus, which opens the way for return and the rebuilding of the house of the LORD. Therefore, the writer does not write a tragedy without a way out; the destruction is not the end of the promise. References: 2 Chronicles 36:15-23.

An ancient tradition attributes it to Samuel, while modern studies discuss stages of collection, editing, and Deuteronomistic interpretation. The book explains repeated defeats not as God's failure, but as Israel's abandonment of the LORD and worship of other gods, while highlighting His mercy when the people cry out to Him.
لا يذكر السفر كاتبًا محددًا، ويشير إلى س: The book does not name a particular author, and refers to royal records such as the Book of the Acts of Solomon and the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel and Judah. The final author reads history in light of the principles of Deuteronomy, explaining division, downfall, idolatry, and exile as covenantal realities, not merely political ones.

Jewish tradition attributed the work to Ezra, while scholarly studies use the expression 'the Chronicler' or 'the Historian' and discuss stages of collection and editing. The genealogies point to a post-exilic community, and many scholars favor the final composition in the Persian period, approximately in the second half of the fifth century B.C., with the precise date remaining a matter of discussion.
لا يذكر النص كاتبًا نهائيًا محددًا، ويبد: The text does not name a specific final author, and it appears to have gathered traditions and historical records within a framework that interprets the transition from the judges to monarchy. The events take place at the end of the period of the judges and the beginning of the reigns of Saul and David, and the book addresses Israel to show that the king must submit to God's word, rather than being an independent political solution.
لا يصرح السفر بأن يشوع كتب جميع مواده، ل: The book does not state that Joshua wrote all its material, so we distinguish between its connection to his testimony and the final composition of the text. The book addresses the people of Israel and later generations to declare that the land is bound to God's promise to the fathers, and that possession does not remove the responsibility of faithfulness to the covenant.

The message may be summarized thus: God sees His people, hears their cry, redeems them, brings them into covenant, and dwells in their midst. The theological trajectory is: slavery ← redemption ← covenant ← holiness ← dwelling.

وقعت الأحداث «في أيام حكم القضاة»، لكن ا: The events occurred «in the days when the judges ruled», but amid the turmoil of Judges, the book presents a story of faithfulness, mercy, and redemption. It begins with famine and death and ends with offspring and the name of David, explaining one of the origins of David's family and showing God's work in daily details. Reference: Ruth 1:1.
يأخذ داود بثشبع ويدبر موت أوريا، فيواجهه: David takes Bathsheba and arranges Uriah’s death, and Nathan confronts him, saying: “You are the man.” David confesses, but forgiveness does not remove temporal consequences, and turmoil enters his house. The narrative makes clear that David’s election does not make him a sinless man, but highlights the importance of confession, repentance, and submission to God’s word. References: 2 Samuel 11–12; Psalm 51.
يبدأ السفر الثاني بسليمان وحكمته وبناء ا: The second book begins with Solomon and his wisdom and the building of the temple and its dedication and the bringing in of the ark and the appearance of the glory of the LORD. Solomon's prayer comes as a forward-looking prayer for sin and drought and war and exile, connecting the temple to repentance and the seeking of God's face, not to the building alone. References: 2 Chronicles 1–7.
يبدأ السفر بعد نهاية التكوين، حين صار نس: The book begins after the end of Genesis, when Jacob's descendants had become numerous in Egypt and a new king arose who did not know Joseph. The book was directed to Israel to explain the origin of its identity: the promise to the patriarchs, Egyptian slavery, God's redemption, the Sinai covenant, and then God's presence in the midst of the community.
يتحول وعد الأرض إلى أسماء ومدن وحدود وتو: The promise of the land becomes names, cities, boundaries, and distribution among the tribes, while the cities of refuge and the Levitical cities present the picture of an ordered society rather than merely a military victory. At Shechem, Joshua reviews salvation history and calls the people to faithfulness: “But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” References: Joshua 13–21; 24:1-15.
يثبت السفر أن الهيكل والازدهار لا يعوضان: The book establishes that the temple and prosperity do not compensate for a heart far from God, and that human kings fail. Yet the promise of God to David remains a door of hope, and the lifting of Jehoiachin from prison at the end of the book indicates that the story is not finished. This repeated failure leads to the expectation of the perfect king from the seed of David. References: 2 Kings 25:27-30; Matthew 1:1; Luke 1:32-33.
يحاول بالاق استخدام بلعام ضد إسرائيل، لك: Balak attempts to use Balaam against Israel, but the curse is turned into a blessing, and Balaam's prophecy presents the image of the star coming forth from Jacob. Then the second census declares the emergence of a new generation, and Joshua is appointed as Moses' successor. The leader changes, but God's promise continues. References: Numbers 22–24; 26–27.
يحمل الكهنة تابوت العهد ويتقدمون إلى الأ: The priests carry the ark of the covenant and go before the people into the Jordan, and the water becomes a path for the people. Rahab hides the spies and declares her acknowledgment of the LORD’s deeds, showing that faith is not measured by national origin alone. Joshua sets up twelve memorial stones to teach the children about God’s work. References: Joshua 2–4; Matthew 1:5; Hebrews 11:31.
يخاطب السفر شعب العهد، ويمنحه جذوره في ا: The book addresses the covenant people and gives them their roots in creation, the patriarchs, and the promise. It declares that God is the Creator and sovereign Lord of the universe, explains the entry of sin and death, and then shows the beginning of the plan of blessing for the nations through the call of Abraham. References: Genesis 1–3; 12:1-3.
يربط أخبار الأيام بين آدم والأنساب وداود: Chronicles connects Adam and the genealogies and David and the temple and worship, then reveals that even the best kings die and do not achieve perfection. The question remains about the king whose kingdom has no end, and the New Covenant comes to proclaim Jesus, the Son of David, with the meaning of God's presence moving to a greater level in Christ. References: 1 Chronicles 17:11-14; Matthew 1:1; Luke 1:32-33.
يركز أخبار الأيام على ملوك يهوذا والإصلا: Chronicles focuses on the kings of Judah and reform and worship. Jehoshaphat appears in teaching the people, Hezekiah in opening the temple and cleansing it and restoring Passover, Manasseh in humility and return, and Josiah in reform after hearing the Law. These narratives reveal that restoration requires prayer and humility and the word of God. References: 2 Chronicles 17; 29–31; 33:10-20; 34–35.
يرى السفر مذلة الشعب ويسمع صراخه ويذكر ع: The book sees the humiliation of the people, hears their cry, and remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The account of redemption reaches its climax in Passover, where the lamb, blood, passing over, and deliverance are connected, after which God opens the way through the sea. Salvation here is not merely political independence, but liberation for worship and entry into God's covenant. References: Exodus 2:23-25; 3:7-10; 12:1-32; 14.
يسلم موسى القيادة إلى يشوع ويشجعه، ثم يص: Moses hands leadership to Joshua and encourages him, then ascends Mount Nebo and sees the land without entering it. Moses dies, but the leader changes while God's purpose does not change; the promise continues through the new generation and Joshua's leadership. References: Deuteronomy 31:1-8; 34:1-12.
يشوع (יְהוֹשֻׁעַ؛ Yehoshua) يعني «الرب ي: Joshua (יְהוֹשֻׁעַ; Yehoshua) means “the LORD saves.” The book follows Deuteronomy directly: Moses dies on the borders of the land, and Joshua leads the people across the Jordan into the beginning of the possession of Canaan. Joshua son of Nun was from the tribe of Ephraim, and one of the two spies who remained steadfast in faith. References: Numbers 13:16; Deuteronomy 34:1-9; Joshua 1:1-9.
يشوع 1–5: القيادة وعبور الأردن والجلجال؛: Joshua 1–5: leadership, crossing the Jordan, and Gilgal; 6–12: Jericho, Ai, and the wars; 13–21: the division of the land and the Levitical and refuge cities; 22–24: the altar of the tribes, covenant renewal, and the death of Joshua. References: Joshua 1–5; 6–12; 13–21; 22–24.

يضع التعداد الأول الرجال القادرين على ال: The first census registers the men able to go to war, and the tribe of Levi is set apart for the service of the tabernacle. The tribes surround the tent of meeting, so that God's presence becomes the center of the nation's identity. When they set out, the movement of the camp is linked to the cloud, the trumpets, and the Lord's direction; the wilderness is a school in which the people learn that food, water, the way, and protection come from God.
يضع موسى أمام الشعب الحياة والموت والبرك: Moses sets before the people life and death, blessing and curse, and calls them to choose life. The text does not present choice as a slogan separate from the covenant, but connects it with loving the Lord, listening to His voice, and keeping His commandments. Reference: Deuteronomy 30:15-20.
يطبق بوعز حق الفقير والغريب في الحقل برح: Boaz applies the right of the poor and the stranger in the field with mercy, then fulfills the role of the kinsman-redeemer (גֹּאֵל) before the elders at the city gate, without bypassing the nearer kinsman. The story combines mercy and justice, and restores the family’s name and land within the legal framework. References: Ruth 2:1-23; 3–4.
يطلب السفر عبادة الرب وحده، ويضع حدودًا: The book calls for worship of the Lord alone and sets limits for the king, prophet, priest, and judge, so that all are subject to the word of God. It also cares for the sojourner, orphan, widow, and slave, because Israel was a slave and a sojourner in Egypt; memory that does not produce mercy is incomplete memory. References: Deuteronomy 12:1-14; 16:18-20; 17:14-20; 24:17-22.
يطلب سليمان قلبًا فهيمًا، ثم يبني الهيكل: Solomon asks for an understanding heart, then builds the temple and dedicates it in Jerusalem. The prayer of dedication affirms that the heavens cannot contain God; the temple is a place God chose to reveal His presence, not a building that confines Him or a talisman that protects a disobedient people. References: 1 Kings 3:5-14; 5–8.
يظهر عثنيئيل نموذجًا مبكرًا للخلاص، وأهو: Othniel appears as an early model of deliverance, Ehud in confrontation with Moab, Deborah and Barak in confrontation with Sisera, Gideon with his small army against Midian, Jephthah in his complexity, and Samson in his strength and downfall. The book does not idealize its heroes; God uses limited leaders, but their limitations do not become a standard of perfection.
يعرض السفر المحرقة، والتقدمة، وذبيحة الس: The book presents the burnt offering, grain offering, peace offering, sin offering, and guilt offering, each with its own context and function. It then consecrates Aaron and his sons to the priesthood, showing that service before the sanctuary is a calling within the covenant order, not an independent human privilege. Leviticus 17:11 explains the centrality of blood in atonement, an important background for understanding New Testament language concerning redemption.
يعيد 1 أخبار 17 عرض عهد الله مع داود، وي: 1 Chronicles 17 presents the covenant of God with David again, linking the seed, the throne, and the temple. God does not allow David to build the temple, but he prepares gold, silver, bronze, wood, and stones and the system of service, and the leader learns to lay a foundation for a project he may not see completed. References: 1 Chronicles 17; 22:1-19; 28–29.
يكشف التذمر والمن والسلوى حنينًا مشوهًا: Grumbling, manna, and quail reveal a distorted longing for Egypt and distrust of God's provision. In the story of the spies, Joshua and Caleb see the land in the light of the promise, while the people believe their fear; God therefore judges the rejecting generation not to enter the land. Then Korah's rebellion shows that religious ambition does not become service merely by drawing near to the sanctuary. References: Numbers 11–14; 16.
يمسح صموئيل داود بن يسى في بيت لحم، ويعل: Samuel anoints David son of Jesse in Bethlehem, and the LORD declares that people look at the eyes, but the LORD looks at the heart. David defeats Goliath not by the strength of weapons alone but by his confidence that the battle belongs to the LORD, then waits for God’s timing and refuses to kill Saul despite the opportunity. References: 1 Samuel 16–17; 24; 26.
يمكن تلخيص الرسالة هكذا: الشعب الذي خلصه: The message may be summarized thus: the people whom God saved and called into covenant must live in holiness before the holy God. The system of sacrifices, priesthood, and atonement provides the framework the New Testament uses to understand Christ as the perfect sacrifice, the great high priest, and the final atonement, without turning every detail into an independent symbol. References: John 1:29; Hebrews 9–10.
ينتهي العدد في سهول موآب، ويبدأ التثنية: Numbers ends on the plains of Moab, and Deuteronomy begins from nearly the same region. In Numbers, we see the people in the wilderness under testing; Deuteronomy places them on the threshold and turns the history of failure into a lesson in obedience. It is therefore the theological threshold between journeying and possession.
ينسب التقليد اليهودي والمسيحي السفر إلى: Jewish and Christian tradition attributes the book to Moses as part of the Torah, while modern academic scholarship discusses the stages in the formation, compilation, and editing of the Torah's texts. Tradition affirms this, but the text alone does not settle every detail of the history of composition; therefore, both views are presented without turning either into undocumented certainty.

Jewish and Christian tradition attributes the book to Moses, who appears as the principal speaker, covenant mediator, and teacher. The book does not provide a calendar date for his birth, and states that he died at the age of one hundred and twenty on Mount Nebo. The final chapter records his death; therefore, scholars discuss its completion and editing in light of tradition and modern study. Reference: Deuteronomy 34:1-7.

Jewish and Christian tradition attributes the book to Moses, who appears as leader, mediator, and prophet. The events begin at Sinai after the exodus and proceed to the plains of Moab opposite Jericho. The book does not specify a calendar year for Moses' birth, and it is established that he died at the age of one hundred and twenty, according to Deuteronomy 34:7.

Jewish and Christian tradition attributes the book to Moses, and its chapters present Moses as a mediator who receives the word of the Lord and conveys it to the priests and the congregation. The events take place in the wilderness after the exodus, centering on the tent of meeting before entry into the land of Canaan. The text does not provide an absolute calendar date, and what is established in biblical tradition is that Moses died at the age of one hundred and twenty, according to Deuteronomy 34:7.
ينسب التقليد اليهودي والمسيحي سفر الخروج: Jewish and Christian tradition attributes Exodus to Moses as part of the Torah. Moses' name in the narrative is associated with his being drawn out of the water, though there is linguistic discussion concerning its possible Egyptian origin. Scripture does not provide a chronological date for his birth or death; it is certain that he died at the age of one hundred and twenty according to Deuteronomy 34:7. As for the date of the Exodus, studies propose multiple models; therefore, no single date is presented as an indisputable fact.
ينقسم السفر إلى التاريخ الأول للبشرية في: The book is divided into the primeval history of humanity in Genesis 1–11, followed by the patriarchal history in Genesis 12–50. The narrative moves from Eden and Mesopotamia to Ur, Haran, and Canaan, and then Egypt, distinguishing between confirmed locations and locations whose identification remains debated.
يواجه إيليا أخاب وإيزابل وعبادة البعل، و: Elijah confronts Ahab, Jezebel, and the worship of Baal, declaring the name 'YHWH is God' as the heart of his message. On Mount Carmel, fire falls after prayer, then comes rain, but Elijah himself passes through exhaustion and despair and experiences God's presence in stillness. References: 1 Kings 17–19.
يولد عوبيد، ثم يسي، ثم داود؛ فتظهر العنا: Obed is born, then Jesse, then David; thus divine providence appears through hunger, work, harvest, marriage, and birth. The book mentions no visible miracle, yet it declares that God works faithfully in the lives of ordinary people. Ruth enters the genealogy of Christ according to Matthew 1:5, while Boaz remains a limited type of the redeemer, not equal to Christ.
